'''Edward Brinton''' (January 12, 1924 &ndash; January 13, 2010) was a professor of [[oceanography]] and research [[biologist]].  His particular area of expertise was Euphausiids or [[krill]], small shrimp-like creatures found in all the oceans of the world.

==Early life==
Brinton was born on January 12, 1924, in Richmond, Indiana to a [[Religious Society of Friends|Quaker]] couple, [[Howard Brinton]] and [[Anna Cox Brinton|Anna Shipley Cox Brinton]].  Much of his childhood was spent on the grounds of [[Mills College]] where his mother was Dean of Faculty<ref>{{cite web | url = https://archive.org/stream/careerhigheredu00bennrich/careerhigheredu00bennrich_djvu.txt | title = A career in higher education: Mills College, 1935-1974: oral history transcript, 1986 | year = 1987 | access-date = 2010-01-23}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine| url=http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,798797-2,00.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100227024656/http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,798797-2,00.html | url-status=dead | archive-date=February 27, 2010 | magazine=Time | title=Religion: Pendle Hill | date=1948-06-21 | access-date=2010-05-01}}</ref> and his father was a professor.  The family later moved to the [[Pendle Hill Quaker Center for Study and Contemplation]], in Pennsylvania where his father and mother became directors.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.pendlehill.org/vision-mission-and-history/90-pendle-hill-beginnings?start=1 | title = Religion: Pendle Hill | date = 1948-06-21 | access-date = 2010-01-23 | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20100108130218/http://www.pendlehill.org/vision-mission-and-history/90-pendle-hill-beginnings?start=1 | archive-date = 2010-01-08 }}</ref>

==Academic career==
Brinton attended High School at [[Westtown School]] in Chester County, Pennsylvania.  He studied at [[Haverford College]] and graduated in 1949 with a bachelor's degree in biology. He enrolled at [[Scripps Institution of Oceanography]] as a graduate student in 1950 and was awarded a Ph.D. in 1957.  He continued on as a research biologist in the Marine Life Research Group, part of the [[CalCOFI]] program. He soon turned his dissertation into a major publication, The Distribution of Pacific [[Euphausiids]].<ref>{{cite journal |author=E. Brinton |title=The distribution of Pacific euphausiids |journal=Bull. Scripps Inst. Oceanogr. |volume=8 |issue=2 |pages=51–270 |year=1962 |url=http://repositories.cdlib.org/sio/bulletin/8no2/}}</ref><ref name="escholarship">{{Cite web|url=http://www.escholarship.org/uc/item/3xq6r58k|title = Bulletin of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography Bibliography|date = 12 December 2007|last1 = Brueggeman|first1 = Peter}}</ref> In this large monograph, he laid out the major biogeographic provinces of the Pacific (and part of the Atlantic), large-scale patterns of pelagic diversity and one of the most rational hypotheses for the mechanism of sympatric, oceanic speciation. In all of these studies the role of physical oceanography and circulation played a prominent part. His work has since been validated by others<ref>{{cite journal | journal =Evolution | volume = 59 | issue = 11 | pages = 2378&ndash;2398 | year = 2005 | doi = 10.1554/05-077.1 | first = Erica| last = Goetze | title = Global Population Genetic Structure and Biogeography of the Oceanic Copepods Eucalanus Hyalinus and E. Spinifer | pmid=16396179| s2cid = 33626909 }}</ref> and continues, to this day, to form the basis for our attempts to understand large-scale [[pelagic]] ecology and the role of physics of the movement of water in the regulation of pelagic ecosystems.<ref>{{cite journal | journal = Can. J. Fish. Aquat. Sci. | volume = 57 | issue =S3  | pages = 16&ndash;23 | year = 2000 | doi = 10.1139/cjfas-57-S3-16 | title = Krill: a possible model for investigating the effects of ocean currents on the genetic structure of a pelagic invertebrate| first1 =Lorenzo | last1 =Zane | first2 = Tomaso | last2 =Patarnello | url = http://rparticle.web-p.cisti.nrc.ca/rparticle/AbstractTemplateServlet?calyLang=eng&journal=cjfas&volume=57&year=2000&issue=S3&msno=f00-166| url-access = subscription }}</ref> In addition to these studies he has led in the studies of how climatic variations have led to the large variations in the California Current, and its populations and communities. He has described several new species and, in collaboration with Margaret Knight, worked out the complicated life histories of many Euphausiid species.<ref>{{cite book |author1=E. Brinton |author2=M. D. Ohman |author3=A. W. Townsend |author4=M. D. Knight |author5=A. L. Bridgeman |url=http://species-identification.org/species.php?species_group=euphausiids&menuentry=inleiding |title=Euphausiids of the World Ocean |publisher=World Biodiversity Database CD-ROM Series, [[Springer Verlag]] |year=2000 |isbn=3-540-14673-3}}</ref> He received a formal tribute from the international [[GLOBEC]] program in 2009.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://web.pml.ac.uk/globec/products/OSM3/presentations/WD/WD_Tuesday%201600_discussion.pdf | title = Tribute to three distinguished krill biologists: Edward Brington, Margaret D. Knight, John Mauchline }}{{dead link|date=November 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> He served as a major adviser and scientist for the State Department-sponsored Naga expeditions in the Gulf of Thailand<ref>{{cite journal |author=E. Brinton |title=Euphausiids of Southeast Asian waters |journal=Naga Report, Part 5. |volume=4 |issue=5 |year=1975 |url=http://www.escholarship.org/uc/item/90g09364}}</ref> and, later, as the curator of the [[UNESCO]]-sponsored Indian Ocean Biological Center in Cochin, India.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.nio.org/userfiles/file/annual_report/1966-67_150.pdf | title = Annual report 1966-1967| publisher = National Institute of Oceanography India | access-date = 2010-01-23}}</ref>  He taught numerous students in both venues. His Academic career continued at Scripps until his retirement in the 1991.

==Family life==
Brinton met and married Desiree Ward in 1948.  He had four children and was widowed in 1976.  He remained unmarried until the time of his death.  His primary residence was in La Jolla, California. He and his family lived in [[Bangkok]], Thailand for a year in 1960, and in [[Kerala]], India from 1965 to 1967.  He died after a long illness on January 13, 2010.<ref>[http://scrippsnews.ucsd.edu/Releases/?releaseID=1042 Obituary] [[Scripps Institution of Oceanography]]. Retrieved 2010-01-26.</ref>
